title: From coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to continuum models of biomolecular condensation
summary: Biomolecular condensation contributes to cellular organization and the regulation of numerous biochemical processes. Capturing its dynamics on large spatio-temporal scales requires a macroscopic model that accurately describes both thermodynamic forces and molecular transport. Here, we investigate the applicability of the Cahn-Hilliard equation for modeling phase-separation dynamics in intrinsically disordered proteins. Using the low-complexity domain of FUS as a model system for biomolecular condensation, we perform coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to infer the free-energy functional and mobility coefficient entering the Cahn-Hilliard equation. The resulting continuum model accurately describes the growth of initial concentration fluctuations in the spinodal regime and the subsequent morphological evolution of the concentration fields during coarsening. We find that the free-energy functional is transferable across different stages of phase separation, whereas the mobility is not. During coarsening, we identify two kinetic regimes characterized by distinct mobilities, which persist even when a concentration-dependent mobility is introduced.

title: Identification and targeting of a novel drug pocket in the tumour angiogenesis regulator RhoJ
summary: The Rho GTPase RhoJ is a key regulator of tumour angiogenesis and has been identified as a target for anti-angiogenic drug design. Its high sequence conservation with the related Rho GTPase Cdc42 complicates selective drug discovery. RhoJ has a unique N-terminal extension (Asn2-Lys19) that is absent in Cdc42 and other Rho GTPases. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations to identify a novel allosteric pocket formed by the RhoJ N-terminus and show that this pocket contributes to interactions with key downstream signalling partners. Structure-based virtual screening of small molecules targeting this pocket identified the antifungal terconazole as a potential binder. Computational docking revealed that terconazole occupies the N-terminal pocket, sharing critical contacts with the interface between RhoJ and PAK3, a key interacting partner. To validate this, we developed an optimized bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (eBRET2)-based biosensor to monitor the interaction between RhoJ and PAK3 in live cells and saw that terconazole disrupted the RhoJ:PAK3 interaction in a dose-dependent manner. Together, our MD results show that the RhoJ N-terminal extension assumes structure on binding to PAK3 and contributes to that interaction, while our cellular biosensor data support targeting this pocket to modulate the RhoJ:PAK3 interaction. The ability of terconazole to bind to the N-terminal pocket and disrupt PAK3 binding provides proof of concept for the specific targeting of RhoJ in the development of novel anti-angiogenic drugs.

title: Decoding Clade-Specific bNAb-HIV-1 Env Interactions Using Machine Learning
summary: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) exhibits extensive genetic diversity, posing a major challenge to AIDS vaccine development. Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) isolated from HIV-1-infected individuals offer valuable templates for designing broadly protective immunogens. Here, structural and energetic descriptors extracted from experimentally resolved bNAb/HIV-1 Envelope (Env) protein-protein complexes were used to develop machine-learning (ML) models predicting binding free energies ({triangleup}G) and dissociation constants (KD) across multiple HIV-1 clades. Among the algorithms evaluated, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) achieved the best predictive performance, with training and test R2 values of 0.92 and 0.658, respectively. Applying the optimized model to HIV-1 datasets revealed clade-dependent binding patterns, with clade B showing the greatest variability and clade G exhibiting signatures associated with reduced neutralization potency. Predicted {triangleup}G of different bNAb classes followed the trend gp120-gp41 interface {approx} fusion domain > CD4 binding site (CD4bs) > V1V2 loop {approx} V3-glycan, consistent with experimentally reported affinity profiles of benchmark bNAbs. Clade C exhibited intermediate {triangleup}G with PGT121, VRC01, and 10-1074 maintaining high-affinity interactions, whereas PG9 and 2G12 show reduced binding affinity. These findings offer quantitative insight into clade-specific bNAb binding energetics and demonstrate the potential of machine-learning approaches to guide HIV-1 immunogen design and vaccine development.

title: Evaluation and primer for using DeepLabCut to track small animals in large spaces
summary: DeepLabCut (DLC), a machine learning-based pose estimation tool, has dramatically increased the throughput of behavioral tracking. Yet its implication remains limited by lack of validation data from diverse scenarios and users' unfamiliarity with the machine learning workflow. Here, we provide a practical primer on DLC terminology and workflow and performance evaluation of DLC in a novel scenario where the target is much smaller than those in previous validation data. We assessed model performance in a total of 36 model configurations across three training proportions, six training iterations, and two recording resolutions. Performance was evaluated on training convergence, prediction error, prediction certainty, and generalizability. Additionally, we selected an optimal model based on a balance between model performance and training time and applied it to 20 recordings at each resolution. In the test frames, 15 and 6 out of 18 model configurations met all performance criteria under high- and low-resolution, respectively. Of these, DLC was able to achieve low prediction error, high prediction confidence, and low train-test loss. Prediction error and confidence varied with training proportion, iteration, and resolution. Inference using the optimal models achieved similar high confidence predictions, with low-likelihood predictions predominantly associated with visual obstruction, low light, and reduced contrast between the subject and the background. Notably, the optimal models for high- and low-resolutions performed similarly despite a multi-fold difference in the cost of the recording devices, providing validation data for DLC in low-budget research, teaching and outreach scenarios.

title: Nucleotide State Regulates Asymmetric Substrate-Binding Protein Docking in a Type II ABC Importer
summary: Type II ABC importers rely on substrate-binding proteins (SBP) to capture nutrients and deliver them to membrane-embedded transporters, but how ATP binding and hydrolysis regulate their interactions remains poorly understood. To address these questions, we determined structures of the Type II small-substrate molybdate importer MolBC-A from H. influenzae in distinct nucleotide-bound states, complemented by molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and functional assays. In a nucleotide-free state, the MolA-MolBC interface is remodeled into a more open conformation, whereas ATP and AMP-PNP binding induce asymmetric conformational changes that preserve the MolA Lobe I interface and disrupt contacts with MolA Lobe II, revealing a previously unresolved partially-docked state. In the ADP-bound state, MolA exhibits the greatest conformational heterogeneity with reduced stable engagement that extends across both lobes. Together these findings define a nucleotide-dependent cycle of asymmetric MolA remodeling and reveal distinct contributions of the two SBP lobes in coupling transporter nucleotide state to SBP engagement.

title: Nanoscopic Origin of Enhanced Tyrosine-Mediated Water Ordering over Canonical Threonine Motifs in a Bacterial Ice-Nucleating Protein
summary: Bacterial ice-nucleating proteins (INPs) are known as the most efficient biological heterogeneous ice nucleators. Ice-nucleation ability is conventionally attributed to the threonine-based conserved motifs of {beta} -helical INPs, whereas the role of other conserved motifs remains overlooked. To identify the motif with the highest hydration-ordering ability, a 16-loop model INP and its two mutants are simulated using all-atom molecular dynamics at 260 K, just below the ice nucleation temperature, using the CHARMM36m force field and TIP4P/Ice water model. Among four potential ice-nucleating sites present in four exposed surfaces of the {beta} -helical INP, the glycine-tyrosine-glycine (GYG) motif-associated interface water (IW) exhibits the probability distribution of the Steinhardt bond-orientational and tetrahedral order parameters closest to that of the Ih. The GYG arrange themselves into a ladder-like array of tyrosine hydroxyls, compatible with the Ih-like lattice geometry, suggesting that this motif provides the IW a favorable template for ice-like water organization. The Y-to-phenylalanine mutation produces the largest disruption in IW order compared to the threonine mutations. Although the difference in entropy of threonine-associated IW and Ih is the least among all sites, ice-like hydration ordering near GYG may exceed prior assumptions for a threonine-based ice-nucleating surface. The ordering is collectively determined by lattice compatibility, entropy reduction, hydrophobicity, interfacial geometry, and sequence conservation. The study unfolds a molecular framework of biological ice nucleation and provides a foundation for the rational engineering of more efficient artificial ice-nucleators for applications in climate-related technologies.

title: Inter- and intra-individual trajectories of brain sex in different neuroendocrine profiles
summary: Sex hormone fluctuations modulate structural and functional brain dynamics, yet little is known on how sex steroid levels map onto the expression of sex differences in the brain. Here, we trained machine learning models for brain sex classification based on magnetic resonance imaging regional volumes in cross-sectional data of N = 1090 individuals (50% females, age matched). Applied to densely sampled data of one male and two females in different hormonal states (naturally cycling, oral contraceptive user, pregnancy), we associated inter- and intra-individual fluctuations in brain sex with neuroendocrine profiles. We found lower variation in brain sex across scan sessions in the male compared to the female subjects. Oral contraceptive use was associated with a more female-like brain, while opposite brain sex trajectories emerged across menstrual cycle phases and pregnancy trimesters. Overall, our findings suggest that changes in brain sex capture hormone-related plasticity over time in densely sampled individuals.

title: Two Pleckstrin homology domains scaffold SNAP-47-containing SNARE complexes
summary: Long-term potentiation requires the regulated insertion of AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane of neurons, a process mediated by a SNARE complex containing SNAP-47, syntaxin-3, and synaptobrevin-2. Compared to other SNAP proteins, SNAP-47 exhibits slower fusion kinetics and contains uncharacterized regions whose functions remain unclear. Here, we integrated biochemical approaches with artificial intelligence structure prediction tools and molecular dynamics to investigate the architecture of SNAP-47-containing SNARE complexes. AlphaFold3 predictions of the ternary SNAP-47-containing SNARE complex revealed one known Pleckstrin homology domain (PH1) and one previously unidentified PH domain (PH2), which we validated experimentally. BioEmu and molecular dynamics simulations indicated that PH1 and PH2 form a stable and energetically favorable interface. In this bound state, PH1 stably interacted with the SNARE coiled coil, and in silico acetylation at a lysine whose acetylation is known to impair SNAP-47 function disrupted this PH1-SNARE interface. AMPAR insertion via SNAP-47-containing SNARE complexes is triggered by the calcium sensor synaptotagmin, and we observed that PH1, PH2, and synaptotagmin-1 can simultaneously engage with the plasma membrane, consistent with a pro-fusion conformation. Together, we provide new mechanistic insight into how PH domains regulate SNAP-47-mediated membrane fusion during synaptic plasticity.

title: Adaptive-optics lattice light-sheet microscopy enables correlative single-molecule imaging of endogenous proteins in native environments
summary: Resolving molecular organization and dynamics in native environments remains challenging, as single-molecule imaging requires high sensitivity and spatiotemporal resolution while preserving 3D cellular context. Here, we present ALPINE (Adaptive-optics Lattice light-sheet microscopy for endogenous Protein Imaging in Native Environments), a modular framework for quantitative single-molecule imaging into complex biological samples. ALPINE combines adaptive-optics lattice light-sheet microscopy, programmable PSF shaping and acquisition stabilization, an engineered cell-specific labelling toolkit for endogenous cell-surface proteins and analysis pipelines assigning molecular localizations and trajectories to 3D cellular compartments. Labelling endogenous AMPA receptors in intact brain tissue, we demonstrate aberration-corrected 3D single-molecule localization and nanoscale organization within neuronal compartments. Importantly, fast optical sectioning of lattice light-sheet illumination further enables 3D single-molecule tracking in live tissue and quantification of molecular dynamics within native cellular environment. Together, ALPINE provides a modular approach to investigate how endogenous molecules are organized and dynamically regulated in complex biological systems, with components adaptable to diverse biological questions and imaging modalities.
